rows.stem: Name the diseases and their mode of transmission in human by (i) common round worm and (ii) filarial worm.
rows.solution:
(i) **Common round worm (Ascaris):** the disease is **ascariasis**. It spreads through **contaminated water, food, vegetables and soil**: the eggs of the parasite are passed out with the faeces of an infected person and contaminate soil, water and plants, and a healthy person picks them up by eating or drinking these.

(ii) **Filarial worm (Wuchereria):** the disease is **elephantiasis (filariasis)**. It spreads through the **bite of the female mosquito (Culex)**, the vector that carries the worm from an infected person to a healthy one.

rows.stem: Explain the role of 'B' and 'T' lymphocytes in providing immunity to humans.
rows.solution:
Both kinds of lymphocyte bring about the acquired immune response, but in different ways:

- **B-lymphocytes** produce an army of proteins called **antibodies** in our blood in response to pathogens. Because the antibodies are found in the blood, this response is called **humoral immunity** (antibody-mediated immunity).
- **T-lymphocytes** do not secrete antibodies themselves, but they **help the B-cells produce them**. They are also responsible for **cell-mediated immunity (CMI)**, for example in the rejection of a transplanted organ.

rows.stem: Plasmodium enters the human body through the bite of infected female Anopheles. Trace its life cycle till the onset of malaria in human.
rows.solution:
The life cycle of Plasmodium in the human body, from the bite to the onset of malaria:

- When an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites a human, the parasite enters the body as **sporozoites** (the infectious form), injected with the bite.
- The sporozoites **reach the liver through the blood**.
- In the **liver cells** the parasite **reproduces asexually**, bursting the liver cells and **releasing the parasites into the blood**.
- The parasites then **enter the red blood cells (RBCs)** and again **reproduce asexually**, bursting the RBCs. Released parasites go on to infect new red blood cells.
- The rupture of the RBCs releases a toxic substance, **haemozoin**, which is responsible for the **chill and high fever recurring every three to four days**. This is the onset of malaria.

The marking scheme also accepts this as the NCERT labelled diagram of the stages in the human host: sporozoites injected with the bite, sporozoites reaching the liver through the blood, asexual reproduction in liver cells with release into the blood, and asexual reproduction in red blood cells causing cycles of fever.

rows.stem:
(a) "For ethical reasons, biodiversity must be conserved." Do you agree ? Write your views in support of your answer.
(b) Write the characteristic features of a specific area on the basis of which it is designated as a "hot spot". Write any one major threat to these areas.
rows.solution:
(a) **Yes**, biodiversity must be conserved for ethical reasons. In support:
- We share this planet with **millions of plant, animal and microbe species**.
- **Every species has an intrinsic value**, even if it is of no current or economic value to us.
- We have a **moral duty to take care of their well-being** and to **pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations**.

(b) A region is designated a biodiversity **hotspot** on the basis of:
- a **very high level of species richness**, and
- a **high degree of endemism**, that is, many species confined to that region and found nowhere else.

A major threat to these areas is **accelerated habitat loss**.
